ytring.label: Freedom to speak up
ytring.desc: Whether you dare to speak up — about mistakes, about disagreement, about what is not working — and whether anything happens when you do. It is not the same as everyone agreeing.
ytring.s1: I can report censurable conditions without fearing consequences
ytring.s2: When someone reports a problem, something is done about it
ytring.s3: Disagreement is raised openly here, not in the corridor afterwards
ytring.name: Freedom to speak up

mengde.label: Workload and time pressure
mengde.desc: The relationship between what has to be done and the time, people and equipment you actually have. Sustained imbalance is the most common cause of health-damaging strain.
mengde.s1: My workload is manageable over time
mengde.s2: I have enough time to do the job well enough
mengde.s3: I can switch off from work when the working day is over
mengde.name: Workload

motstrid.label: Conflicting demands
motstrid.desc: When two managers, two systems or two concerns ask for things that do not go together, and no one says what should give way.
motstrid.s1: I rarely get tasks without knowing what should be deprioritised
motstrid.s2: The demands from different quarters hang together
motstrid.s3: I know who decides when two things collide
motstrid.name: Conflicting demands

kontakt.label: Contact and communication
kontakt.desc: Whether the work allows contact with others. Working alone brings both social isolation and a safety risk — you must be able to call for help.
kontakt.s1: I have the opportunity for contact with colleagues during the working day
kontakt.s2: I can call for help quickly if something happens while I am alone
kontakt.s3: I do not feel isolated in my job
kontakt.name: Contact and communication

emosjon.label: Emotional demands
emosjon.desc: The strain of facing demanding encounters with people — customers, users, colleagues — or of having to conceal your own reactions.
emosjon.s1: I am rarely left alone in emotionally demanding situations
emosjon.s2: We talk about difficult incidents afterwards
emosjon.s3: I am allowed to react as a human being at work
emosjon.name: Emotional demands

leder.label: Support from manager
leder.desc: Whether the manager is available when things get difficult, and whether the support is practical rather than merely well-meaning.
leder.s1: I get support from my manager when the job becomes demanding
leder.s2: My manager knows enough about what my job actually involves
leder.s3: I can raise difficult matters with my manager
leder.name: Support from manager

medvirk.label: Participation and control
medvirk.desc: Influence over your own working day: order, pace, method — and over changes that affect you.
medvirk.s1: I have influence over how I carry out my work
medvirk.s2: I am heard when something is to be changed
medvirk.s3: I can influence the pace of my own work
medvirk.name: Participation

integritet.label: Integrity and dignity
integritet.desc: Whether people are met with respect and equality, whether their boundaries are upheld, and whether they may exercise their own professional and ethical judgement. This is also the legal basis for protection against harassment.
integritet.s1: I am met with respect regardless of who I am
integritet.s2: I may use professional judgement when I think something should be done differently
integritet.s3: My boundaries for privacy are respected at work
integritet.name: Integrity and dignity

rolle.label: Role clarity
rolle.desc: Whether you know what is expected, where your responsibility ends, and what counts as good enough.
rolle.s1: I know what is expected of me in my job
rolle.s2: I know where my responsibility ends and others begin
rolle.s3: I know what counts as good work here
rolle.name: Role clarity

kollega.label: Support from colleagues
kollega.desc: Whether people actually turn up for one another in practice, not just in speeches.
kollega.s1: My colleagues turn up when I need help
kollega.s2: We share knowledge instead of holding on to it
kollega.s3: I feel like part of the team
kollega.name: Support from colleagues

mening.label: Recognition and meaning
mening.desc: Whether the work feels meaningful and whether effort is seen by someone who matters.
mening.s3: I am proud to work here
mening.name: Meaning and recognition

rapport.title: Report
rapport.lead: One basis, four recipients. Choose who the report is for — the content changes with it.

audienceNote.tilsyn: Full documentation with legal bases, method, participation and signature fields. This is the version you present at an inspection.
audienceNote.amu: A committee paper with a recommendation and room for the minutes. Without individual comments.
audienceNote.ledelse: Two pages: the figures, the three priorities, and what they cost in time. Without statutory references.
audienceNote.ansatte: Plain language, no figures below the threshold, no quotes that could be traced. Giving this back is what makes people answer next time.

docTitle.tilsyn: Documentation of systematic work on the psychosocial working environment
docTitle.amu: Paper for the working environment committee — psychosocial working environment {year}
docTitle.ansatte: This is what you said — and this is what we are doing

docLead.tilsyn: Prepared under the Working Environment Act § 3-1 (c) and § 4-3, and the regulation on the performance of work, part two chapter 1A. The document covers the survey and risk assessment of the psychosocial working environment — not the undertaking's other health and safety duties. It shows the survey, the risk assessment, the measures and the effect assessment for the period.
docLead.amu: A committee paper with findings, risk assessment and proposed measures. The safety representative and the union representatives have reviewed it before the meeting.
docLead.ledelse: A short account of where the undertaking stands, what weighs it down most, and what has been decided.
docLead.ansatte: Everyone who answered should know what came of it. This is the feedback to the whole undertaking.

basis.head: Legal basis
basis.body: Legal obligation, GDPR art. 6(1)(c), cf. the Working Environment Act §§ 3-1 and 4-3. Not consent — employees cannot consent freely to their employer, and the measurement is a duty in any case.

stored.head: What is stored about each person
stored.body: About employees, only name, e-mail address and mobile number (if you enter it) are stored, and which department they belong to. For each survey, whether the invitation was sent and whether the person has answered is recorded, so that reminders go only to those who have not. Answers are stored without any link to a person: there is no column that could hold one.

special.head: Special categories
special.body: The questions are written to avoid health data, cf. WEA § 9-3. The screening for offensive behaviour and violence is reported as counts only.

retention.head: Retention
retention.body: The data is kept for as long as the agreement lasts. If you cancel, everything is deleted automatically 30 days after the agreement ends: the employee list, the answers, the comments, the measures and the users. While the agreement lasts, individual answers are not deleted automatically.

access.head: Access and erasure
access.body: Register details can be corrected and deleted on request. Anonymous answers cannot be retrieved or deleted individually — they are not identifiable, cf. GDPR art. 11.

processor.head: Processor

forsteTimen.title: The first 60 minutes
forsteTimen.lead: Add people, set the threshold, choose a measurement and send. The shortest route from an empty account to the first round.

body.p1: Start under Settings → People. Paste names, e-mail addresses and groups from the spreadsheet you already have. The order is name, e-mail, group, manager, and a header row is optional. People without a group are imported anyway and land in “No group” — they get the measurement, but their answers cannot be broken down by department.
body.p2: Then check the groups and the threshold. Groups decide what you can break the result down by, and should follow where people actually work together. The threshold decides how many answers it takes before a group is shown on its own. Five is the floor and cannot be lowered.
body.p3: Finally, set the measurement up under Measurement setup. That is where you confirm that the safety representative was consulted and the need discussed with the union representatives — not a checkbox, but the documentation § 9-2 requires. Only then can the round be planned.
body.p4: One thing to know before you send: sending needs a mail integration that is not connected in this installation. The year wheel plans the rounds and queues the notices, but the queue stands until somebody connects sending.

ansatteUtenHr.title: Adding people without an HR system
ansatteUtenHr.lead: Paste from a spreadsheet, import a CSV, or type them in one at a time.

body.p1: Under Settings → People you choose between pasting from a spreadsheet and adding one person at a time. The spreadsheet route is faster above about ten people: select the columns in Excel and paste them. The columns are read as name, e-mail, group and manager, and the separator may be a tab, a semicolon or a comma.
body.p2: Before you import you get a preview of the first four rows and a count of what is wrong — rows without a valid e-mail, and rows without a group. Neither stops the import. A person without an e-mail cannot be reminded, and a person without a group cannot be counted in a department's result, but both get the measurement.
body.p3: E-mail is optional because not everybody uses one during the working day. For them a link or a QR code in the break room works just as well — the answer is stored the same way however the person reached the form.
body.p4: The register is continuously compared with the number of employees you have stated. If it says the register is short, the people missing will not get the measurement, and the response rate is a fraction of a number that is wrong.

velgTerskel.title: Choosing the right threshold for your size
velgTerskel.lead: Why five is the default, what happens to groups below it, and why the floor cannot be lowered.

body.p1: The threshold is how many answers a group must have before its result is shown for that group alone. Below it no figures are shown for the group on its own — its answers count in the whole. When the small groups together have fewer answers than the threshold, the smallest of the other groups is held back too, so that nobody can work them out by subtraction.
body.p2: Five is the default, and in Orgpuls five is also the floor. It is not a setting that can be lowered: the threshold is enforced by a function in the database that always counts at least five, whatever the configuration says. You can raise it to ten if you want to be stricter.
body.p3: The reason is not the Working Environment Act but data protection law. In a group of three a result can in practice be traced back to individuals, and then it is no longer anonymous figures — it is personal data, with a full right of access and erasure.
body.p4: The consequence is worth planning for: with many small departments you get few figures to steer by. Merging groups that actually work together is a better answer than lowering the threshold, which does not work anyway.

grunnlinjeEllerPuls.title: Baseline or pulse — what is the difference
grunnlinjeEllerPuls.lead: The baseline sets the zero point once a year. The pulse measures whether the measures worked. When you need both.

body.p1: A baseline is the whole instrument: eleven factors with three statements each, plus the questions outside the index. It takes a few minutes to answer and gives a complete picture. It is placed in the same month every year, so the figures are comparable over time.
body.p2: A pulse is short. It asks only about the factors that have an open measure — the places where you have already decided to do something. That is the point: a pulse is not a new survey, it is an evaluation of effect.
body.p3: Which factors a pulse asks about is set automatically from which measures are still running. Close a measure and the factor drops out of the next pulse unless something else pulls it in.
body.p4: Most undertakings need both: one baseline a year for the documentation, and three pulses in between to see whether anything moved. That is what the year wheel's default rhythm does.

settOppArshjulet.title: Setting up the year wheel
settOppArshjulet.lead: Fixed rounds, the notification order, and who hears about it when. Why quarterly beats monthly for most.

body.p1: The year wheel is a setup you do once. It decides the rhythm — the baseline only, baseline plus a quarterly pulse, or baseline plus a pulse every month — and which month the baseline falls in.
body.p2: Once it is on, it plans the rounds itself. Every hour it looks for rounds that have become due: a planned round that has reached its opening day is opened, the invitations are queued, the reminder is queued on the day the round is configured with, and a round past its deadline is closed and frozen.
body.p3: The notification order is not optional. Safety and union representatives are notified first, then the managing director, then the department managers, and last everybody. The reason is § 6-2 fourth paragraph: the safety representative must be involved before the survey starts, so a wheel that notified everybody at once would automate a breach. How far in advance the notices go is yours to change.
body.p4: Quarterly beats monthly for most. Four measuring points a year is enough to see whether a measure worked, and rare enough that people still bother to answer.

egneSporsmal.title: Adding your own questions
egneSporsmal.lead: Five is the ceiling. Why they are reported separately, and why the index stays untouched.

body.p1: You can add up to five of your own questions to a measurement. The ceiling is enforced by the database rather than by the form — a sixth question is refused.
body.p2: Your own questions are reported separately and never enter the index. That is not a limitation, it is the whole point: the index is built on a validated instrument with known properties, and a question you wrote yourself does not have those properties. Mixed in, it would make the number incomparable both with last year and with other undertakings.
body.p3: Use them for what the instrument does not cover and that is specific to you — a reorganisation, a new shift system, a move. Avoid questions about health: § 9-3 prohibits an employer from collecting health data, and a well-meant “how are you really doing?” is closer to that line than it looks.
body.p4: A question with empty text is refused, and so is one longer than 300 characters.

svarprosent.title: Getting the response rate up
svarprosent.lead: Tuesday at nine, one reminder, and what matters most: that people saw the last round lead to something.

body.p1: The timing matters more than people think. The year wheel puts the send on the first Tuesday of the month, at nine. Monday competes with the start of the week and Friday sits until after the weekend.
body.p2: One reminder, not three. It goes to those who have not answered, and it is sent by the system — not by the manager. Nobody learns who is missing, and that matters more to the response rate than the reminder itself: people answer more honestly when they know nobody is keeping track of who answered.
body.p3: If you have people without regular e-mail use during the working day, the channel is the single biggest factor. A link in the break room or an SMS moves the response rate more than any wording in the invitation.
body.p4: What matters most is still the last round. Were the findings shared within two weeks, and did anything happen? If not, the response rate falls next time, and that is a rational reaction from people who spent five minutes on something that led nowhere.

lesIndeksen.title: Reading the index correctly
lesIndeksen.lead: What the number means, and why movement matters more than level.

body.p1: The index is an average of the factors, converted to a scale from 0 to 100. An answer of 1 becomes 0, an answer of 5 becomes 100. The number has no absolute meaning — there is no line at which a work environment becomes “good”.
body.p2: Movement is more informative than level. Three points down on one factor while the rest stands still is a signal; that the index is 61 and not 68 is not, unless you know what it was last year.
body.p3: Look at the factors before the total. The total can stand still while two factors move in opposite directions, and those two are the interesting ones.
body.p4: Remember who the number is about. If you are a department manager, the number you see is your own team's, not the whole undertaking's — the screen says which of the two it is.

strekIStedet.title: Why there is a dash instead of a number
strekIStedet.lead: The threshold applies. What you can do — and why you should not lower it to see the number.

body.p1: A dash means the group had fewer answers than the threshold. The number is not hidden from you in particular; it has not been calculated for anyone.
body.p2: It is worth noting that the group is not left out of the whole either. The answers count towards the undertaking's figures — they are just not shown for that group alone.
body.p3: What you can do is merge groups that actually work together, or get the response rate up in that group. What you cannot do is lower the threshold below five: the database always counts at least five whatever the configuration says.
body.p4: The temptation is real, and worth resisting. A number for a group of three is not an anonymous number.

funnTilTiltak.title: From findings to measures
funnTilTiltak.lead: Share the findings within two weeks, hold the meeting, choose three things. The order that decides whether anything happens.

body.p1: Share the findings within two weeks. It is the single thing that decides the response rate next time, and it is also what § 3-1 assumes: a survey that is not shared is not a system, it is a questionnaire.
body.p2: Hold a meeting where the figures are interpreted by the people they are about. The safety representative should be there — not as a formality, but because the interpretation is often where the work is. Two departments with the same figures can have entirely different causes.
body.p3: Choose three things. Not ten. A measure in Orgpuls has an owner, a deadline and a factor it hangs on, and runs through six steps from proposed to closed. A measure cannot be closed before its effect has been measured — the database refuses it.
body.p4: The effect is measured by the next pulse, which asks about exactly the factors that have open measures. That is the loop § 3-1 c describes: survey, assess risk, act, follow up.

hvaVilagrer.title: What we store, and what we do not
hvaVilagrer.lead: The answer is stored with no connection to a person. What that means in practice, for administrators too.

body.p1: About each person we store a name, an e-mail address and a group in the register. That is all.
body.p2: The answer itself is stored in a table that has no column that could hold a link to a person. Not an empty one, not an optional one — none. The row holds which round the answer belongs to, which group the person is in, and which hour it was submitted, truncated to the hour.
body.p3: That applies to administrators as well. There is no view, no export and no query that can answer what a named person answered, because the fact does not exist anywhere. The invitation link is looked up by a cryptographic digest at the moment it is used, and the comparison is not stored.
body.p4: The practical consequence: an individual answer cannot be retrieved on request, and it cannot be deleted individually. GDPR article 11 covers exactly this case — data that can no longer be attributed to a person.

svarPaKommentar.title: Answering an anonymous comment
svarPaKommentar.lead: A two-way conversation without either of you knowing who the other is. When a comment should leave the track.

body.p1: When somebody writes a comment on a statement, they are given a key in their browser. The database stores only a digest of the key, so nobody — not even somebody with database access — can work it out.
body.p2: The person can come back with the key, read your answer and write again. You see a conversation with no sender: “Employee · anonymous”, and nothing else. That is not a fact the screen is hiding — it does not exist.
body.p3: Comments from a group that did not reach the threshold are not shown at all. And the group never travels with a comment that is released: “somebody in the workshop wrote this” is a smaller haystack than the promise can carry.
body.p4: An answer does not have to be a solution. “I have read this and will take it to the management meeting on Thursday” is enough for people to write again next time.

gdpr.title: GDPR: legal basis and retention
gdpr.lead: Legal obligation, not consent. Why that is right, and what you need in place.

body.p1: The legal basis is legal obligation, GDPR article 6(1)(c), cf. the Working Environment Act §§ 3-1 and 4-3. Not consent.
body.p2: That is not a technicality. Consent must be freely given, and an employee cannot consent freely to their employer — the power relationship is uneven. The survey is also a duty the undertaking has in any case, and a consent that cannot be withdrawn without the duty falling away is not a consent.
body.p3: The questions are written to avoid health data, which § 9-3 prohibits an employer from collecting. The screening for offensive behaviour and violence is reported as counts only.
body.p4: Three things must be in place before real answers are processed: a routine for deleting individual answers, a data processing agreement with a list of sub-processors, and an entry in the record of processing activities. The data processing agreement is under Settings › Data processing agreement, where the managing director signs it. You still need to set up the deletion routine and the record yourselves.

hvaLovenKrever.title: What the Working Environment Act actually requires
hvaLovenKrever.lead: § 3-1 c, § 4-3 and chapter 1A of the regulation. What Orgpuls covers, and what you need elsewhere.

body.p1: § 3-1 c requires the undertaking to survey hazards and problems, assess the risk, draw up plans and put measures in place. Orgpuls covers that letter for the psychosocial work environment, and documents all four steps.
body.p2: § 4-3 sets the requirements for the psychosocial work environment, including protection against offensive behaviour. Chapter 1A of the regulation, in force from 1 January 2026, names the factors: role clarity, conflicting demands, emotional demands, workload and support. The instrument measures all of them.
body.p3: The index is not a legal requirement. No provision mentions a number. What is required is that you can document the four steps — and that is what the report produces.
body.p4: This is what Orgpuls does not cover: goals for the work-environment effort, deviation handling, sick-leave follow-up and review of the system itself — letters a, e, f and h. Nor safety rounds, appraisals, training or occupational health services. The survey is one source, and the Labour Inspection Authority expects you to use several.

kontrolltiltak.title: The measurement as a control measure
kontrolltiltak.lead: §§ 9-1 and 9-2: discussion with union representatives, information about duration, regular evaluation.

body.p1: A work-environment measurement is a control measure within the meaning of the Act. § 9-1 requires objective grounds in the undertaking's circumstances, and that the measure does not impose a disproportionate burden.
body.p2: § 9-2 sets three requirements you must be able to show: the need, the design and the implementation must be discussed with the union representatives before the measure is put into effect; employees must be informed of the purpose, the practical consequences and the expected duration; and the measure must be evaluated regularly.
body.p3: Measurement setup stores this as part of the round rather than as a tick. The discussion is recorded with a date and who it was held with, and the safety representative's involvement under § 6-2 is recorded separately.
body.p4: The evaluation has its own cadence on the measurement. It is the part most often forgotten, because it falls due long after everybody has moved on.

rapportTilTilsynet.title: The report to the Labour Inspection Authority
rapportTilTilsynet.lead: What it contains, which period it covers, and what to attach.

body.p1: The report is built to be the documentation an inspection asks for, not a presentation. It follows the four steps of § 3-1 c in order: what was surveyed, what the risk assessment concluded, which measures were put in place, and what the follow-up showed.
body.p2: It covers the period from the round opening to it closing, and uses the figures as they stood when the round was frozen. Figures that can change afterwards do not belong in documentation.
body.p3: The threshold applies here too. Groups below it are not left out of the whole, but are not shown individually, and the report says why rather than letting it look like missing data.
body.p4: Attach what Orgpuls does not have: minutes from the discussion with the union representatives, safety rounds in the period, and documentation of information and training.

rollerOgTilgang.title: Roles and who sees what
rollerOgTilgang.lead: Managing director, department manager, safety representative, union representative. Where the lines are, and why.

body.p1: The managing director sees the whole undertaking, every factor and every anonymous conversation, and can change the settings. Neither means seeing who answered what — that link does not exist for anyone.
body.p2: A department manager sees their own department once the threshold is met, and the conversations from it. Other departments are not hidden, they are absent: a group out of reach is not shown at all, because “Workshop: hidden” would still say the workshop answered, and how many.
body.p3: The safety representative sees the same figures and the same risk assessment as management, and is notified first when a round starts. They do not see individual comments — involvement under § 6-2 is about surveying and measures, not correspondence.
body.p4: Union representative is a position in the register, not a login. It is recorded because § 9-2 requires the discussion to be documentable, and it grants no access in itself. The same holds for the role field in the register generally: it says who somebody is under the act, not what they may read.

entra.title: Connecting Microsoft Entra ID
entra.lead: Which permissions we ask for, which groups sync, and what happens when somebody leaves.

body.p1: The Entra connection is not built in this installation. This article describes what it will require, so that you know what you would be taking on.
body.p2: The permissions are read access to users and groups, and nothing else. No integration in Orgpuls writes back to the source system, and none of them gets access to the answers — they read who works here, not what anybody answered.
body.p3: You choose which groups are synchronised. A group that is not selected does not exist for Orgpuls, and its members do not get the measurement.
body.p4: When somebody leaves the directory, they are taken out of the register. The answers they have already given stay — they are not linked to the person, so there is nothing to remove. Until the connection exists, the register is maintained under Settings → People.

sms.title: Sending by SMS
sms.lead: For people without regular e-mail during the working day. What it will require.

body.p1: SMS sending is not built in this installation. This article describes what it will require.
body.p2: The main requirement is mobile numbers in the register. Settings → Integrations shows how many of the register have one today. Without a number a person cannot be reached by SMS, and falls back to e-mail or a link.
body.p3: The message is short, with a sender name you choose and a personal link appended at the end. The link cannot be used twice, and it says nothing about who answered what.
body.p4: SMS is the channel that moves the response rate most for sites, workshops and shift work. It is billed per message, so it is worth deciding whether it is used for every send or only for the reminders.

anonymous.a: Yes. We never store a name, an e-mail address or an IP address with the answer — there is no column that could hold the link. And no group is shown before at least five people have answered. Below that line there is only a dash, for administrators too. Five is the floor and cannot be set lower.

twelve.q: What if we are only twelve people?
twelve.a: Then you get figures for the whole undertaking, but not broken down by department. That is not a limitation we added, it is a consequence of the numbers: with twelve employees a department of three is recognisable. We could not keep the promise of anonymity.

inspection.q: Does this hold up as documentation if the Labour Inspection Authority comes?
inspection.a: Orgpuls documents the survey and the risk assessment of the psychosocial work environment — the requirement in § 3-1 c of the Working Environment Act. The report shows what was measured, how the risk was assessed, which measures were put in place and whether they worked. Other health-and-safety duties, such as deviation handling and sick leave, you cover elsewhere; we do not.

time.q: How much time does it take us?
time.a: Setup takes under an hour the first time: add the people, choose the threshold and approve the question set. After that the year wheel plans the rounds itself. Employees spend four minutes on the annual survey and under a minute on a pulse.

leaving.q: What happens to the data if we stop using Orgpuls?
leaving.a: You own it. Download everything as PDF at any time, including after a cancellation. If you cancel, we delete the answers after 30 days. The reports you have downloaded you keep, so that the documentation is in order.

home.title: How to use Insight
home.s1: Read the three items under “Waiting for you”. If they are empty, you are up to date.
home.s2: The loop shows where you stand against the legal requirement. If you are stuck on one step, that is where the work is.
home.s2Plain: The loop shows where you stand in the work. If you are stuck on one step, that is where the work is.
home.s3: Switch role at the top right to see exactly what department managers and the safety representative see.
home.s3Plain: Switch role at the top right to see exactly what department managers see.
home.sci: The index is a weighted average of the eleven factors, converted from 1–5 to 0–100. A change of less than three points is within normal variation and should not be read as a trend. Source: QPS Nordic user guide, STAMI.

measure.title: How to use Measurements
measure.s1: The baseline is the statutory one. It is taken once a year and sets the zero point.
measure.s1Plain: The baseline is the big one. It is taken once a year and sets the zero point.
measure.s2: The pulse only measures the factors you have open actions on — it tells you whether the actions work.
measure.s3: The annual cycle does both automatically, with the safety representative notified first.
measure.sci: An annual baseline combined with short pulses gives better data quality than frequent long surveys. Survey fatigue sets in noticeably after about eight questions, and the response rate falls faster than the quality of the answers.

result.title: How to read the result
result.s1: Start with “Do these three”. They are ranked by effect on the whole, not by lowest score.
result.s2: Tap a factor row to see the three statements and the distribution behind the number.
result.s3: “Assess risk” turns the finding into an action with an owner and a deadline.
result.sci: The prioritisation is a driver analysis: how strongly each factor varies with the overall assessment in your organisation specifically. That is why a factor at 64 can rank above one at 52. Based on the job demands–resources model (Bakker and Demerouti).

conv.title: How to handle conversations
conv.s1: Reply even if you do not have a solution. “I have read this” is enough.
conv.s2: If the matter is serious, you can ask for direct contact. The person decides whether to write to you.
conv.s3: Close the conversation when you are done, so it does not keep counting as unanswered.
conv.sci: Getting a reply to an anonymous comment is the single factor that best predicts whether people write again at the next measurement. Unanswered comments lead to a lower response rate next round than having no comment field at all.

tasks.title: How to see actions through
tasks.s1: Every action should have one named owner. Shared responsibility is no responsibility.
tasks.s2: Choose collective actions before individual ones — change the work, not the people.
tasks.s3: An action cannot be closed until its effect has been measured in the next pulse.
tasks.sci: The Labour Inspection Authority and STAMI both point out that actions aimed at how work is organised work better than individual measures such as stress-management courses. Collective actions are to be considered first.

plan.title: How to set up a measurement
plan.s1: Choose the type. A baseline covers the legal requirement, a pulse measures effect.
plan.s1Plain: Choose the type. A baseline gives the whole picture, a pulse measures effect.
plan.s2: Choose factors and comment mode. Fewer questions give a higher response rate.
plan.s3: Check the groups against the threshold, and leave the notice to the safety representative on.
plan.sci: Short pulses take about a minute and typically give a response rate 15–20 percentage points higher than a full form. The questions come in a shuffled order, so people do not answer on autopilot.

wheel.title: How the annual cycle works
wheel.s1: Choose a rhythm. A quarterly pulse is enough for almost everyone.
wheel.s2: Check the notification order — the safety representative and union representatives must always come first.
wheel.s3: Turn on the main switch. Sending, reminders and follow-up then run by themselves.
wheel.sci: Predictability raises the response rate: when employees know the measurement comes in the same month every year, more of them answer. Unannounced measurements are more often read as control than as participation.

settings.title: How to set up the organisation
settings.s1: Add people first — by hand or from a spreadsheet. Everything else builds on the register.
settings.s2: Check the groups and the threshold. Small groups are shown only as part of the whole.
settings.s3: The privacy pages are already filled in. Read them once, and you can answer employees’ questions.
settings.sci: A threshold of five is not arbitrary. With fewer than five answers, results in small groups can in practice be traced back to individuals, and they are then personal data under the GDPR — with full rights of access and erasure.

law.home: The loop on this page is section 3-1 (c) of the Working Environment Act put into a system: survey, assess risk, implement actions, follow up the effect. The index is not a legal requirement — the documentation of the four steps is. The annual cycle covers section 3-1 first paragraph, that the work is to be done in cooperation with employees and union representatives.
law.measure: The Act requires no particular method and no particular frequency. It requires that the survey is sound and repeated when conditions change, cf. section 3-1 (c) and (g). The factors here are the ones section 4-3 and chapter 1A of the Regulations concerning the performance of work name — which is why the wording is locked.
law.result: The risk assessment is the legal requirement itself: section 3-1 (c) says survey “and on this basis assess the risk factors”. A number alone is not a risk assessment. Section 4-1 first paragraph requires the working environment to be assessed “individually and collectively” — hence both factor rows and an overall index.
law.conv: Anonymous comments are not whistleblowing under chapter 2A, but they can contain it. Section 2-3 second paragraph (d) obliges employees to report harassment and discrimination, and section 4-3 third paragraph prohibits it. If you receive such a message, it leaves this track and goes into the organisation’s whistleblowing procedure.
law.tasks: Section 3-1 (c) requires the survey to result in plans and actions — not just in insight. The Labour Inspection Authority and STAMI both point out that collective actions aimed at how work is organised are to be considered before individual ones. That is why an action cannot be closed until its effect has been measured.
law.plan: A recurring measurement with results per group counts as a control measure. Section 9-1 then applies: an objective reason in the organisation’s circumstances, and no disproportionate burden. Section 9-2 requires discussion with union representatives in advance, information to those affected about purpose, consequences and duration, and regular evaluation. Section 6-2 fourth paragraph gives the safety representative the right to be consulted.
law.wheel: Section 3-1 (g) requires “continuous monitoring of the working environment” when the risk factors call for it — not one measurement a year. Letter (h) requires you also to review whether the system itself works. The notification order in the annual cycle covers the participation requirement in section 3-1 first paragraph and section 6-2 fourth paragraph.
law.settings: The threshold is not a requirement of the Working Environment Act but follows from data protection law: with fewer than five answers, results in small groups can be traced back to individuals. The legal basis is legal obligation under GDPR Article 6(1)(c), not consent — employees cannot freely consent to their employer. Section 9-3 also prohibits collecting health information, which is why the questions are designed to avoid it.
law.report: The documentation requirement lies in section 3-1 third paragraph, which provides for regulations on “requirements for documentation of the systematic health, environment and safety work”. Section 7-2 fourth paragraph requires medical information of a personal nature to be removed before the working environment committee considers reports, and the sixth paragraph that the committee submits an annual report to governing bodies, the employees’ organisations and the Labour Inspection Authority.

ytring.ev: Basis: research on psychological safety (Edmondson). What moves the number most is what the leader does in the moment after someone speaks up.

m1.title: Answer every report within five days
m1.how: Every deviation report and every suggestion gets a named answer: what will happen, or why nothing will. No report is left lying.

m2.title: Workshop: What stops us from speaking up?
m2.how: The team writes down, anonymously, situations where they chose not to speak up. The leader listens without defending, and you end with two concrete changes.

m3.title: The leader asks first and speaks last
m3.how: The leader asks for objections before decisions and thanks those who raise them. Disagreement is written down instead of smoothed over.

mengde.ev: Basis: the demand–control–support model (Karasek) and the job demands–resources model (Bakker and Demerouti). Measures work best when the employees themselves help find the solutions.

m1.title: Weekly prioritisation meeting
m1.how: The leader and the team go through everything on the table and agree on what has to give. The result is one written, ranked list.

m2.title: Workshop: Find the time thieves
m2.how: The team logs its work for a week and finds tasks that can be removed, simplified or moved. At least three changes are decided before you leave.

m3.title: Clear limits on when you are available
m3.how: Agree when it is fine to send and answer messages outside working hours. The leader goes first.

motstrid.ev: Basis: research on role conflict. Unclear priorities between several people who order work is a strong source of stress, and it is solved in the organisation, not in the individual.

m1.title: One person decides when two demands collide
m1.how: Settle in writing who has the last word when demands from different directions do not fit together, and make it known to everyone.

m2.title: Workshop: Responsibility map
m2.how: The team maps the most important tasks: who orders, who carries out, who approves. Where two people order, you choose one.

m3.title: A new task in, another one down
m3.how: When the leader hands out a new task, they say at the same time what is to be deprioritised.

kontakt.ev: Basis: social support dampens the effect of high demands (Johnson and Hall). For lone work the regulations also require a way to call for help.

m1.title: An alarm arrangement for lone work
m1.how: Make sure everyone who works alone has a fixed way to call for help, and test that it works.

m2.title: A fixed meeting point for those who work alone
m2.how: A short, fixed meeting, in person or on Teams, where those who work alone meet colleagues and the leader.

m3.title: Buddy arrangement
m3.how: Whoever often works alone gets a fixed colleague to call and discuss matters with.

emosjon.ev: Basis: research on emotional labour (Hochschild). Note: a single debriefing right after an incident has not shown effect in systematic reviews. What works is support from colleagues and follow-up over time.

m1.title: A short talk with colleagues after demanding incidents
m1.how: After a difficult incident those involved have a short, voluntary talk the same day. The leader follows up a few days later.

m2.title: Workshop: When the job gets to us
m2.how: The team shares which situations drain the most, and agrees on how they help each other through them.

m3.title: Nobody stands alone in the hardest meetings
m3.how: Decide which meetings with customers or clients always have two people present.

leder.ev: Basis: studies of leadership development show effect when the training is practical and followed up over time. Regular conversations between leader and employee are one of the simplest moves.

m1.title: A fixed conversation every 14 days
m1.how: Short, fixed conversations where the employee sets the agenda. They get moved, but never cancelled.

m2.title: The leader works a day with the team
m2.how: The leader takes part in the ordinary work for a day to see what the job actually involves.

m3.title: A mentor for new hires
m3.how: An experienced colleague follows up new hires, so the leader is not the only one they can ask.

medvirk.ev: Basis: influence over one's own work is one of the best documented protective factors (Karasek). Job crafting, where employees adjust their own tasks, gives measurable but moderate effects.

m1.title: Workshop: Job crafting
m1.how: Each employee goes through their own tasks and proposes one change in how they are done. The leader says yes, or gives a reason for a no.

m2.title: Those affected are involved before changes are decided
m2.how: Changes that touch the working day are put to those concerned before the decision is made, not after.

m3.title: The team plans its own week
m3.how: The leader sets goals and deadlines. The team decides order and distribution.

integritet.ev: Basis: the bullying research group at the University of Bergen (Einarsen et al.). Early intervention by the leader and clear routines stop conflicts from developing into bullying.

m1.title: Go through the routine for offensive behaviour
m1.how: Show how to report and what happens afterwards. Make sure there is a route around the immediate leader.

m2.title: Workshop: This is how we want it here
m2.how: The team agrees on concrete ground rules for how they speak to and about each other, and what they do when someone crosses the line.

m3.title: The leader steps in early
m3.how: The leader deals with belittling comments and exclusion at once, in a calm conversation, before it becomes a case.

rolle.ev: Basis: role clarity is closely tied to job satisfaction and lower stress, and good training at the start has a lasting effect.

m1.title: An expectations conversation with every employee
m1.how: The leader and the employee write down the three most important areas of responsibility and what counts as good enough.

m2.title: Workshop: Who does what
m2.how: The team goes through the grey zones where it is unclear who is responsible, and assigns them.

m3.title: A training plan for new hires
m3.how: A written plan for what new hires are to learn, from whom, and when they count as fully trained.

kollega.ev: Basis: support from colleagues dampens the effect of high demands. Measures that build support in the daily work do better than one-off social events.

m1.title: Regular learning meetings
m1.how: A colleague shares something they have learnt or solved. Sharing knowledge becomes a habit, not a coincidence.

m2.title: Make asking for help normal
m2.how: The leader asks for help themselves and gives credit to those who step up for others.

m3.title: Workshop: This is how we help each other
m3.how: The team works out when they need each other most, and how to make it easy to get help.

mening.ev: Basis: research shows that contact with those the work benefits raises both motivation and effort (Grant). Recognition works best when it is concrete and comes quickly.

m1.title: Show who the work makes a difference for
m1.how: Share feedback from customers and clients with those who actually did the job.

m2.title: Concrete recognition the same week
m2.how: Praise what was actually done, and say why it mattered. Do not wait for the appraisal.

m3.title: Workshop: What we are proud of
m3.how: The team shares examples of work they are proud of and what made it possible, and works out what you should do more of.

lovkrav.h1: Mapping the psychosocial working environment – without a separate project
lovkrav.lead: The Working Environment Act requires you to map the psychosocial working environment, assess the risk, put measures in place and follow up. Since 1 January 2026 the regulation says more clearly how. Orgpuls makes each step part of work you do anyway.

blocks.text: What the law requires – four steps

The requirement is in section 3-1, second paragraph, letter c of the Working Environment Act: the employer shall map hazards and problems, assess the risks on that basis, draw up plans and implement measures to reduce the risk. For the psychosocial working environment, chapter 1A of the regulation on the performance of work expands on this, in force since 1 January 2026.

items.text: Map, assess risk, make plans and put measures in place. **How Orgpuls does it:** one survey is the mapping, the result shows the risk per factor, and the findings become measures with an owner and a deadline.

The psychosocial working environment shall be fully satisfactory. **How Orgpuls does it:** eleven factors covering what the section names, among them unclear and conflicting demands, emotional demands, workload and support.
Mapping shall be done together with the employees, repeated regularly and documented. **How Orgpuls does it:** the annual wheel plans the rounds, and every round is stored with its date.
The safety representative shall be consulted. **How Orgpuls does it:** the safety representative sees the same figures as management, at no extra cost.

blocks.text: The documentation builds itself

The regulation requires the mapping and risk assessment to be documented and to form part of the systematic health, safety and environment work. In Orgpuls every survey, every risk assessment and every measure is stored with a date and an owner. The report follows the four steps of section 3-1 letter c in order: what was mapped, what the risk assessment concluded, which measures were put in place, and what the follow-up showed.
The figures stay as they were when the round closed, so the documentation does not change afterwards. The report can be printed or saved as PDF the day someone asks.

blocks.title: What Orgpuls does not cover
blocks.text: Orgpuls covers the mapping and risk assessment of the psychosocial working environment. HSE goals, deviation handling, sickness absence follow-up and safety inspections live elsewhere. Arbeidstilsynet expects mapping to draw on several sources – a survey is one of them.
What a year looks like

items.title: Measures
items.text: The result points to what lifts the most. You choose measures and give each an owner and a deadline.

faq.q: Does the mapping requirement apply to small organisations?
faq.a: Yes. Section 3-1 applies to every employer with employees. The regulation says mapping shall be adapted to the organisation's nature, activities and size – a small organisation can keep it simple, but not skip it.

faq.q: Is an employee survey enough?
faq.a: It is a good source, but rarely the only one. Arbeidstilsynet also points to safety inspections and appraisal conversations. What counts is that you map, assess risk, put measures in place and follow up – and can show it.

faq.q: What changed on 1 January 2026?
faq.a: The regulation on the performance of work gained a new chapter 1A on the psychosocial working environment. Arbeidstilsynet writes that the changes bring no new requirements, but clarify the ones that already applied.

faq.q: How often must we map?
faq.a: The regulation says mapping shall be repeated regularly and when changes may affect the risk. It sets no fixed interval. A common rhythm is one main survey a year with short pulses in between.

nyeRegler2026.title: New rules on the psychosocial work environment, 2026 | Orgpuls
nyeRegler2026.description: Since 1 January 2026 the regulation has its own chapter on the psychosocial working environment. What the change means for mapping, measures and documentation.
nyeRegler2026.h1: New rules on the psychosocial working environment from 1 January 2026
nyeRegler2026.lead: On 1 January 2026 the regulation on the performance of work gained a new chapter 1A on the psychosocial working environment. Arbeidstilsynet says the requirements are not new, but are now written more clearly. For many organisations it is still a good reason to look at how they map.

blocks.text: In short

items: Chapter 1A of the regulation on the performance of work applies from 1 January 2026.
The employer shall map psychosocial working environment factors, assess the risk and put measures in place.
Mapping shall be done together with the employees and their representatives, repeated regularly and documented.
According to Arbeidstilsynet the rules clarify requirements that already applied – they introduce no new ones.

blocks.text: What the regulation actually says

Chapter 1A has five sections: a fully satisfactory psychosocial working environment (§ 1A-1), mapping and risk assessment (§ 1A-2), measures (§ 1A-3), information and training (§ 1A-4) and the employee's duty to take part (§ 1A-5). In practice, § 1A-2 and § 1A-3 matter most.
The employer shall map psychosocial working environment factors that may affect the employees' health, safety or welfare.
blocks.cite: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-2, first paragraph (our translation)

blocks.text: The employer shall then assess the risk of harmful effects, both in the short and the long term. The risk assessment shall cover the factors one by one, how they affect each other, and whether together they amount to a risk.
Four requirements for how it is done
The fourth paragraph of § 1A-2 says the mapping and risk assessment shall be:

items: carried out together with the employees and their representatives
adapted to the organisation's nature, activities and size
repeated regularly and when changes may matter for the risk in the organisation
documented and part of the organisation's systematic health, safety and environment work

blocks.text: § 1A-3 follows on: on the basis of the risk assessment the employer shall draw up the necessary plans and implement the necessary measures to remove or reduce the risk. That too shall be done together with the employees and their representatives.
What is new, and what is not?

The duty to map and assess risk is not new. It is in section 3-1 of the Working Environment Act, and section 4-3 requires the psychosocial working environment to be fully satisfactory. What is new is that the regulation describes how: that the factors are to be assessed one by one and together, and that the work is to be repeated and documented.

Section 4-3, second paragraph, of the Act names among other things unclear or conflicting demands and expectations, emotional demands in work with people, workload and time pressure, and support and help at work. Those are the factors a good mapping should cover.

blocks.title: Three questions to ask internally
blocks.text: When did we last map the psychosocial working environment? Who took part – the safety representative and the union representatives? And can we show what happened to the findings? If any of the answers is unclear, that is where to start.
What this means in practice
1. Look at the factors one by one – and together

One overall wellbeing score is not enough. The regulation asks you to look at the factors one by one and at how they interact. A high workload is one thing. A high workload combined with little support from the manager is a different and bigger risk.
2. Involve the safety and union representatives from the start

Working together means more than reporting the result afterwards. Under section 6-2 of the Working Environment Act the safety representative shall be consulted during the planning and implementation of measures. Let the safety representative see the same basis as management. Read more about [the safety representative's role in mapping](/artikler/verneombudets-rolle-i-kartleggingen).
3. Make it a rhythm

«Repeated regularly», it says, but the regulation sets no fixed interval. Many choose one main survey a year with short pulses in between, so they can see whether the measures work. Read more in [How often should you measure the working environment?](/artikler/hvor-ofte-bor-dere-male-arbeidsmiljoet)
4. Document as you go

The documentation shall be part of the systematic HSE work. The simplest way is for it to be produced while you work: what was measured, what you assessed, which measures you chose, who owns them, and what the next survey showed.
How Orgpuls covers the requirements
Information, training and the employees' duty

§ 1A-4 says the employer shall give employees the necessary information about the risk factors and the measures put in place, and ensure the necessary training. In practice the result of the mapping cannot stay with management. Employees shall know what came out, and what will be done.

§ 1A-5 goes the other way: employees themselves have a duty to take part in the work for a fully satisfactory psychosocial working environment, with reference to section 2-3 of the Working Environment Act. Answering the mapping and taking part in the follow-up is part of that.
Common questions about the change
Do we have to change tools or write new routines?

Not necessarily. If you already map the psychosocial working environment, assess risk, put measures in place and document it, you are on the right track. Go through the four requirements in the fourth paragraph of § 1A-2 and see whether anything is missing – often it is the follow-up and the documentation.
Does it apply to small organisations?

Yes. The rules apply to every employer. Mapping shall be adapted to the organisation's nature, activities and size, so an organisation of ten can keep it simpler than one of two hundred – but cannot skip it.
Is an annual employee survey enough?

It can be a good part of the mapping, but it rarely covers everything. Arbeidstilsynet recommends several sources, for example safety inspections and appraisal conversations. And a survey without risk assessment, measures and follow-up does not meet the requirement on its own.

Orgpuls measures eleven psychosocial factors with three statements each, and shows the risk per factor. The findings become measures with an owner and a deadline, and short pulses measure whether the measures work. The safety representative sees the same figures as management. Everything is stored with a date, and the report follows the steps of section 3-1 letter c. See [what the law requires, and how Orgpuls does it](/lovkrav).

kravKartlegging.title: Requirements for mapping the work environment | Orgpuls
kravKartlegging.description: The Working Environment Act requires every organisation to map the psychosocial working environment. The four steps, who should take part, and common mistakes.
kravKartlegging.h1: Requirements for mapping the psychosocial working environment
kravKartlegging.lead: Every organisation with employees shall map the psychosocial working environment, assess the risk, put measures in place and follow up. The requirement is in section 3-1 of the Working Environment Act and is expanded on in the regulation on the performance of work. Here is what it means, step by step.

blocks.text: The short answer

The employer shall map hazards and problems in the working environment, assess the risk, make plans and put measures in place. That includes the psychosocial side – workload, role clarity, support, speaking up and the like. The work shall be done together with the employees and their union representatives, repeated regularly and documented.
Where is the requirement?

items.text: The employer shall ensure systematic health, safety and environment work at every level of the organisation, together with the employees and their union representatives.
Map hazards and problems, assess the risks, draw up plans and implement measures to reduce the risk.
The psychosocial working environment shall be fully satisfactory. The second paragraph names among other things unclear demands, emotional demands, workload and support.
Mapping and risk assessment of the psychosocial factors – together, adapted to the organisation, repeated regularly and documented.
The safety representative shall see to it that the psychosocial working environment is safeguarded, and be consulted on measures.

blocks.text: The four steps
1. Map

Find out how employees experience the working environment. An anonymous survey is the most common tool, but Arbeidstilsynet recommends several sources, for example safety inspections and appraisal conversations. The mapping should cover what section 4-3 names: demands and expectations, emotional demands, workload and time pressure, support, integrity and dignity, contact with others, and protection from harassment.
2. Assess the risk

What do the findings mean? Where is the risk that people get ill, leave or stop speaking up? The regulation asks you to look at the factors one by one, at how they affect each other, and at whether together they amount to a risk – in both the short and the long term.
3. Put measures in place

Choose measures that remove or reduce the risk, and give each measure an owner and a deadline. Arbeidstilsynet writes that collective measures should be considered before individual ones, and mentions among others clear role descriptions and regular meetings with the manager.
4. Follow up
Did the measure work? You only know when you measure again. Many skip this step, and that is why the next mapping often shows the same as the last.

blocks.title: Three findings, not nine
blocks.text: A mapping that produces ten measures usually produces none. Choose the two or three findings that matter most, do them properly, and measure whether they worked before taking on the next.
Who should take part?

Mapping is the employer's responsibility, but it shall be done together with the employees and their representatives. In practice this means the safety representative and the union representatives help plan the mapping, see the result and take part when measures are chosen. If the organisation has a working environment committee – required where at least 30 people are regularly employed, and between 10 and 30 if one of the parties demands it – the work naturally belongs there too.

Many organisations treat a work environment survey as a control measure under chapter 9 of the Working Environment Act, and therefore discuss its purpose, design and implementation with the union representatives before sending it. It is a good principle in any case: people answer a survey more honestly when they know why they are getting it.
Common mistakes

items: **Measuring without acting.** The findings are presented and then nothing happens. Next time the response rate falls.
**Measures without an owner.** «We will get better at communicating» is not a measure. «The department head introduces a weekly board meeting from 1 March» is.
**No follow-up.** A measure is not done until the next survey shows whether it worked.
**Small groups that can be recognised.** Figures for a department of three are not anonymous. Set a lower limit, and keep it.
**No documentation.** If you cannot show what you did, in practice it is as if it was not done.

blocks.text: Checklist before you start

items: Decide who takes part: management, the safety representative and the union representatives.
Tell employees about the purpose, the anonymity and when the result will come.
Choose a tool that covers the factors in section 4-3 and has a fixed anonymity limit.
Set aside time to go through the result within two weeks of the survey closing.
Choose two or three measures with an owner and a deadline.
Plan the next survey before you close this one.

blocks.text: What the documentation should contain
The regulation says the mapping and risk assessment shall be documented, but not in what form. Good documentation answers what an inspector or a new safety representative will ask:

items: When the mapping was done, and who helped plan it
How it was done: method, who was asked, and the response rate
What came out, factor by factor
How the risk was assessed, and what was prioritised
Which measures were chosen, with owner and deadline
What the follow-up showed – whether the measures worked

blocks.text: Attach what does not come from the survey: minutes from the discussion with the union representatives, safety inspections in the period, and how employees were told about the result.

Orgpuls covers the four steps for the psychosocial working environment and documents them while you work. Read more about [the legal requirement and how Orgpuls meets it](/lovkrav), or about [the new rules from 2026](/artikler/nye-regler-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo-2026).

sporsmal.description: Which questions belong in an employee survey? The topics that matter, eleven example questions with an answer scale, and why fewer questions give better answers.
sporsmal.h1: Employee survey: the questions that give answers
sporsmal.lead: A good employee survey is short, covers what actually affects the working environment, and asks questions people can answer honestly. Here are the topics to include, example questions and what to do with the answers.

blocks.text: Fewer questions give better answers

It is tempting to ask about everything. But every question costs time, and fatigue gives worse answers towards the end. More importantly: every question quietly promises that someone will act on the answer. Only ask what you are willing to follow up.
A main survey of around 30 statements takes about four minutes to answer. Short pulses between main surveys should take under a minute.
The topics to include

Section 4-3 of the Working Environment Act and chapter 1A of the regulation on the performance of work point to the factors that matter most for the psychosocial working environment. A survey used for mapping should cover them:

head: Topic
What it is about
rows: Whether the tasks and the time available are in balance
Whether people know what is expected, and where their responsibility ends
Whether demands from different directions fit together
The strain of working with people, and whether anyone shares it with you
Whether the manager steps in when the job gets demanding
Whether people help each other and share knowledge
Whether it is safe to speak up – and whether anything happens when you do
Whether people have a say over their own work
Whether people are treated with respect
Whether people have contact with others during the working day
Whether effort is noticed, and whether the work feels meaningful

blocks.text: Eleven example questions

The questions work best as statements people take a position on, on a five-point scale: **strongly disagree, somewhat disagree, neither, somewhat agree, strongly agree**. Here is one statement per topic, as they appear in Orgpuls (translated):

items: I can speak up about unacceptable conditions without fearing the consequences
My workload is manageable over time
I rarely get tasks without knowing what should be deprioritised
I can be in contact with colleagues during the working day
I am rarely left alone in emotionally demanding situations
I get support from my manager when the job gets demanding
I have a say in how I carry out my work
I am treated with respect whoever I am
I know what is expected of me in my job
My colleagues step in when I need help
The work I do matters

blocks.title: Write statements, not questions
blocks.text: «I know what is expected of me in my job» is easier to answer honestly than «Is your role clear?». The statement is concrete, is about one's own experience and has no right answer.
Questions outside the index
Some questions do not fit an overall index, but are worth asking:

items: **Recommendation:** «How likely is it that you would recommend us as a workplace to someone you know?» Reported as a figure of its own.

**Offensive behaviour:** «Have you experienced or witnessed offensive behaviour, harassment or bullying at work in the last twelve months?» Should only be shown as a count for the whole organisation, never per group.

blocks.text: An open comment field often gives the most important findings. But free text can reveal who wrote it, even when no name is stored. Treat comments with the same care as figures for small groups.
Working in construction, or in health and care? See the [industry modules](/bransjer): question sets that go one layer deeper where your workplace is different, in addition to the main survey.
Anonymity: why a limit of five answers

People answer honestly when they know the answer cannot be traced back. That takes more than not storing the name: a department of three people is recognisable regardless. So no group should be shown until a minimum has answered. In Orgpuls the limit is five, and it cannot be lowered. Read more in [Anonymous employee survey: what does anonymous mean?](/artikler/anonym-medarbeiderundersokelse)
What to do with the answers

The result is not the answer – it is the start of a conversation. Share it with employees within two weeks. Choose the two or three findings that matter most and turn them into measures with an owner and a deadline. Do not take on nine things at once.
How to read the result

In Orgpuls the answers are converted to an index from 0 to 100: strongly disagree becomes 0, strongly agree becomes 100, and each factor gets the average of its three statements. A factor at 65 or above counts as low risk, 50–64 as medium and below 50 as high.

The level is still less interesting than the movement. A factor at 61 says little on its own. A fall from 64 to 61 since last year, while the rest stand still, is a signal. Look at the factors before the total – the total can stand still while two factors move in opposite directions.
Why five answer options

A five-point scale with a midpoint lets people say «neither» when that is what they mean. Without a midpoint they are forced to take a side, and that adds noise. More steps rarely give better data – the difference between 6 and 7 on a ten-point scale means different things to different people.

Then measure again on the factors where measures are running. You see whether anything has moved, and employees see that their answers led somewhere. That is what keeps the response rate up next time.

hvorOfte.h1: How often should you measure the working environment?
hvorOfte.lead: The short answer: one main survey a year, and short pulses in between. The main survey documents the state. The pulses show whether the measures work. Here is why – and what an annual wheel can look like.

blocks.text: What the rules say

The Working Environment Act sets no fixed interval. Section 1A-2 of the regulation on the performance of work says the mapping and risk assessment shall be repeated regularly and when changes may matter for the risk in the organisation. A reorganisation, a merger, a new system or a demanding period is therefore a reason to map again, whenever you last did it.
One survey a year shows a state, not a direction

An annual survey gives a snapshot. It tells you where you stand, but not whether last year's measures worked, because so much else has happened between two surveys. Twelve months is also a long time to wait to know whether something helped.
When a year passes between each time, the survey also becomes a project. It is planned, presented and forgotten. That is the most common reason work on the working environment stalls.
Baseline and pulse

items.title: Baseline – once a year
items.text: The full question set. Sets the zero point and documents the mapping. Put it in the same month every year, so the figures can be compared.

items.title: Pulse – between baselines
items.text: A few statements, only on the factors where you have put measures in place. The pulse is not a new mapping, but a measurement of whether the measure works.

blocks.text: An example annual wheel

head: Month
What
Time per employee
rows: Review, risk assessment and measures with an owner and a deadline
Pulse on the factors with open measures

blocks.text: July is holiday, and December is busy for many. Keep the surveys out of both.
How long can a pulse be?

Short. A pulse that takes more than a couple of minutes starts to feel like a new survey, and then the response rate falls. Keep it to the factors where a measure is running – often two or three factors with three statements each – and it takes under a minute.
What about the response rate?

More frequent surveys do not lower the response rate by themselves. What makes the response rate fall is people not seeing that the last round led to anything. When the findings are shared and the measures are visible, it is easier to get people to answer again.

items: Send at the same time every time, for example the first Tuesday of the month at nine.
Send one reminder, not three – and let the system send it, not the manager.
Use SMS or a QR code where people do not sit at a PC.
Say what happened after the last round before you send the next.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Measure as often as you can follow up. A survey you do not have time to act on is worse than none.
When to measure outside the rhythm
The rules mention changes that may matter for the risk. Typical examples:

items: reorganisation, a merger or downsizing
new management or new managers across much of the organisation
a move, new premises or a shift to working from home
new systems or ways of working that change the day for many
a demanding event or period – an accident, a conflict, a large project

blocks.text: Then it is better to map the affected factors now than to wait for the next baseline. A pulse aimed at, say, workload and role clarity can do the job.
Compare like with like

A baseline should be compared with the previous baseline, ideally measured in the same month. A pulse is compared with the pulse before. Mix the two and you compare different question sets – and then a change may be due to the questions, not the working environment.
Small organisations

In a small organisation it is tempting to drop the pulses. But that is exactly where they are cheapest: a few statements, under a minute per person. Remember that no group should be shown under five answers. If you are few, you see the figures for the whole organisation, not per department.

In Orgpuls the annual wheel plans the rounds itself: one baseline a year and pulses in between, where the pulse only asks about the factors with open measures. Read more about [the questions to include](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse-sporsmal).

anonym.title: Anonymous employee survey: what does anonymous mean?
anonym.description: When is an employee survey really anonymous? Why the name is not enough, why small groups must be hidden, and what to ask the supplier.
anonym.h1: Anonymous employee survey: what does anonymous mean?
anonym.lead: Not storing the name is not enough. A survey is only anonymous when nobody can work out who answered what – not from the data, not from small groups, and not from what is written in a comment. Here is what it takes.

blocks.text: Why anonymity decides the quality

People answer honestly when they are confident the answer cannot be traced back. If they are in doubt, they answer politely – or not at all. A survey with doubtful anonymity gives figures that look good but are not true.
Three ways anonymity breaks
1. The answer can be linked to the person

Many tools send a personal link and store who has answered, so they can send reminders. If that link sits alongside the answers, anonymity is a promise, not a property. Ask whether the answer is stored with anything that could identify the person who gave it: name, e-mail, IP address or an exact time.
2. The group is too small

A department of three is recognisable even if no name is written anywhere. The solution is a lower limit: no group is shown until a minimum has answered. Five is common. The limit must apply to everyone – administrators too – and it should not be possible to lower it to «see the figure anyway».
3. You can calculate your way there

This is the one most often overlooked. If you see the figure for the whole organisation and for every department but one, you can calculate the last. Then it does not help that the small department is hidden. A good tool therefore holds back one more department when that is needed so the sum does not add up.

blocks.title: Why is there a dash?
blocks.text: A dash instead of a number means the group had too few answers. The figure is not hidden from you in particular – it is not calculated for anyone. The answers still count in the whole.
Comments are the hardest

Free text can reveal who wrote it, even when no name is stored. «As the only woman in the workshop …» needs no signature. Comments should therefore only be shown when the group has enough answers, and management should be able to reply without learning who they are replying to.
Anonymous, but still a conversation

Anonymity does not have to mean one-way communication. In Orgpuls (the Usual plan) management can reply to a comment without knowing who wrote it. The writer gets a private link and can read the reply and answer back – without anyone learning who it was.
Questions to ask the supplier

items: Is the answer stored with a name, e-mail, IP address or exact time?
What is the smallest group that is shown – and can an administrator lower the limit?
Does the tool prevent calculating your way to a hidden group?
How are comments from small groups handled?
Where is the data stored, and is it shared with anyone?

blocks.text: How Orgpuls does it

items: The answer is stored without name, e-mail or IP address, and the time is rounded to the hour. There is no column that could hold a link.
No group is shown until at least five have answered. The limit lives in the database and cannot be lowered, only raised.
When the figures for the other groups would reveal a hidden group, one more group is held back.
Answers are stored in the EU and are not shared with third parties.

blocks.text: Reminders without knowing who is missing

Reminders raise the response rate, but they are also where anonymity most often leaks. If the manager sends reminders, the manager must know who has not answered – and then also who has. The fix is for the system to send the reminder, once, and for the list of who is missing to be unreadable by anyone in the organisation.
How to explain anonymity to employees
People believe in anonymity when it is explained concretely, not when they are given a promise. A short text before the survey goes out can read like this:

blocks.title: Example text
blocks.text: «Your answers are stored without name, e-mail or IP address. No group is shown until at least five have answered – not even to management. There is no list of who answered what, and nobody can make one. We get the figures, not you.»
Also say what happens with the result, and when. Anonymity makes people safe enough to answer. Seeing something happen afterwards makes them bother.
Read also about [the questions to include](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse-sporsmal), or see how anonymity works [when you are few](/smaa-bedrifter).
